candidate.answerReason: The sum of the two real cube roots is exactly 1, and every numerical choice A through D exceeds 1.

methods.label: Find an equation for the sum
methods.explanation:
The radicands have a simple sum and product, so keep the individual cube roots unnamed numerically. Let
\[
u=\sqrt[3]{5+2\sqrt{13}},
\qquad
v=\sqrt[3]{5-2\sqrt{13}},
\]
where both cube roots are real. Then
\[
u^3+v^3=10,
\qquad
(uv)^3=(5+2\sqrt{13})(5-2\sqrt{13})=-27.
\]
The unique real cube root of \(-27\) is \(-3\), so \(uv=-3\).

Set \(t=u+v\). Expanding its cube combines the known sum and product:
\[
t^3=u^3+v^3+3uv(u+v)=10-9t.
\]
Thus
\[
0=t^3+9t-10=(t-1)(t^2+t+10).
\]
For every real \(t\),
\[
t^2+t+10=\left(t+\frac12\right)^2+\frac{39}{4}>0.
\]
Therefore \(t=1\).

Choices A and D exceed \(1\). Choice B exceeds \(1\) because \(65>4^3\), and choice C exceeds \(1\) because \(\sqrt[6]{13}>1\). Hence the sum is \(\boxed1\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses real cube-root uniqueness, elementary polynomial identities, and positivity of a square.

methods.label: Recognize cubes of square-root expressions
methods.explanation:
The pair of radicands differs only in the sign of \(\sqrt{13}\), suggesting that their cube roots might also form such a pair. Cubing \(1\pm\sqrt{13}\) gives
\[
(1\pm\sqrt{13})^3
=1\pm3\sqrt{13}+39\pm13\sqrt{13}
=40\pm16\sqrt{13}.
\]
Both terms have a factor of \(8\), so
\[
\left(\frac{1\pm\sqrt{13}}2\right)^3
=5\pm2\sqrt{13}.
\]
Every real number has exactly one real cube root. This identifies both roots, including the negative root of \(5-2\sqrt{13}\), and their sum is
\[
\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}2+\frac{1-\sqrt{13}}2=\boxed1.
\]
Choices A and D are greater than \(1\); B is greater than \(1\) since \(65>64\); and C is greater than \(1\) since \(\sqrt[6]{13}>1\). The answer is therefore \(\mathrm{E}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses direct multiplication of real square-root expressions to identify the cube roots exactly.
